title: How US Companies Work
summary: Ownership, reporting and governance basics that shape every US client's priorities: public vs private, quarterly earnings, activists, boards and private equity. Knowing who the client answers to tells you which answer they can actually accept.

blocks.title: Who owns the client changes the question
blocks.body: A US public company answers to thousands of shareholders and reports every quarter. A family-owned private firm can think in decades. A PE-owned company has a sponsor with a fixed holding period and a lot of debt. The same 'grow profits' prompt means a different time horizon, risk appetite and cash constraint for each. Ask about ownership early; it frames every recommendation.

blocks.title: Ownership types at a glance
rows: Cost-out, pricing, add-on acquisitions, exit readiness

blocks.title: The public-company reporting rhythm
items: 10-Q: quarterly financial report filed with the SEC; 10-K: annual report with audited financials and risk factors.
8-K: filed for material events between reports (CEO exit, big acquisition, guidance change).
Earnings call: CEO and CFO present results, then analysts ask questions live; stock can move sharply the next day.
Guidance: management's forecast for next quarter or year; missing your own guidance hurts more than missing analyst estimates.
Consensus: the average of sell-side analyst estimates; 'beat' or 'miss' is judged against it.

blocks.title: How US CEOs and CFOs talk
items: EPS (earnings per share): the headline number; buybacks raise EPS by shrinking share count even with flat profit.
Margins: gross, operating and EBITDA margin; 'margin expansion' is a favorite promise.
Same-store / comparable sales: growth from existing locations, stripping out new openings.
Free cash flow: cash after capex; funds dividends, buybacks and M&A.
'Returning capital to shareholders': dividends plus share repurchases.
Adjusted / non-GAAP figures: exclude one-offs; always ask what was adjusted out.

blocks.title: Short-termism is real but not the whole story
blocks.body: Quarterly pressure can push managers to cut R&D or marketing to hit a number. But markets also reward credible long-term plans (think large tech capex cycles). In a case, flag the tension: a recommendation that dents next year's EPS needs a clear payback story the board can defend to investors.

blocks.title: Boards and activist investors
blocks.body: The board hires, pays and can fire the CEO, approves big deals and represents shareholders. NYSE and Nasdaq rules generally require a majority of independent directors. Activist hedge funds buy a stake, then push publicly for change: sell a division, cut costs, return cash, replace directors. A proxy fight is when the activist asks shareholders to vote its nominees onto the board. Activist pressure often triggers consulting work on portfolio and cost.

blocks.title: Private equity and LBOs in one minute
items: LBO: buy a company using mostly borrowed money secured on its own cash flows; equity is the smaller slice.
Value creation levers: EBITDA growth, multiple expansion at exit, and paying down debt.
The sponsor plans an exit (sale to strategic buyer, another PE fund, or IPO) within a set window.
High debt means cash flow and covenants matter; capex-heavy or slow-payback ideas are hard to sell.
Commercial due diligence (CDD) for PE buyers is a large source of consulting work.

blocks.title: Fiscal years and the Fortune 500
items: Many firms use the calendar year, but not all: big retailers often end around late January, after holiday returns.
Microsoft's fiscal year ends June 30; Apple's ends late September. Always check which quarter is 'Q4'.
The US federal government's fiscal year runs October 1 to September 30.
Fortune 500: US companies ranked by annual revenue. The 2026 list needed ~$7.5B revenue to qualify; combined revenue was ~$21T.
Amazon topped the 2026 list, ending Walmart's long run at No. 1.

blocks.title: India vs US: corporate context
rows: Promoter families and business groups often hold controlling stakes
Widely held; institutional investors (index funds, pensions) dominate
Quarterly 10-Q, annual 10-K, earnings calls with live analyst Q&A
Established; activist campaigns are routine news
Control buyouts with leverage are mainstream
April to March for most firms
Mostly calendar year, with notable exceptions

blocks.title: Use the vocabulary naturally
blocks.body: When you size an initiative, translate it: 'This adds ~$40M of EBITDA, about 2 points of margin, which the CEO can put in front of analysts.' Linking operations to EPS, margin or exit multiple shows you understand what a US executive is actually judged on.

in_a_case: PE-owned client: anchor on the exit. Prioritize moves that lift EBITDA within the hold period and avoid long-payback capex; ask how much leverage and when the sponsor plans to sell.
Public company with flat stock price: check whether an activist is circling; portfolio pruning, cost-out and capital return become likely asks.
Retail client 'Q4' result: confirm the fiscal calendar before comparing quarters; a retailer's Q4 may include the holidays and January.
If your recommendation hurts near-term EPS, pair it with a payback timeline and investor narrative the board can defend on the earnings call.
Fit conversation: tying your Indian audit or startup work to US terms (EPS, EBITDA, guidance) signals you can talk to US executives on day one.

flashcards.back: 10-K: annual report with audited financials. 10-Q: quarterly report. 8-K: filed for material events between reports.
Management's own forecast for the next quarter or year; missing it is a credibility hit.
They reduce shares outstanding, so EPS rises even if total profit is flat.
